A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a well-child checkup. The patient and his mother both state that the patient has been otherwise well except for occasional mild pain and stiffness in the upper back. Symptoms began gradually about a year ago and are present intermittently. The pain and stiffness do not bother him significantly or limit his activities, and they have never awakened him from sleep. He denies any trauma or overuse. He is not currently playing any organized sports although he is able to be normally active with friends and siblings.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient feels well except for occasional upper back pain and stiffness. No fever, chills, or night sweats. No weight loss or change in appetite. He is not yet shaving, and his voice has not yet changed.

Skin: Mild acne, no other rash or lesions.

HEENT: No vision changes, ear pain, hearing changes, neck stiffness, or pain in the throat.

Pulmonary: No shortness of breath or cough.

Cardiovascular: No chest pain or pressure.

Gastrointestinal: No diarrhea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. Normal bowel movement once a day.

Genitourinary: No dysuria or increased urinary frequency.

Musculoskeletal: Positive for intermittent upper back stiffness and discomfort. No joint swelling or discomfort.

Neurologic: No numbness, tingling, or pain running down his arms or legs. No weakness or gait changes. No difficulty controlling bladder or bowels.

Psychiatric: No depression, psychosis, or hyperactivity.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Uncomplicated birth, no hospitalizations.

Surgical history: None

Medications: None

Allergies: Penicillin (rash)

Family history: His father had diabetes and hypertension and died when patient was very young. His maternal grandmother died of breast cancer at age 76 years. There is no history of skeletal dysplasia or muscular dystrophy in the family.

Social history: Patient was born at 37 weeks' gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery and had an uncomplicated postnatal course. He is in age-appropriate grade in school and doing well academically and behaviorally. On interview with the mother outside the room, the patient reports that he feels happy and supported at home with his mother and sisters. Patient reports that he has never tried alcohol, drugs, or cigarettes. He is not sexually active.

The patient's family is from Guinea Bissau but the patient was born and raised in the United States and has not traveled outside the country. No known history of tuberculosis exposure. He is up to date on all vaccinations, and he received an influenza vaccine this year. He eats a normal diet, including fruits and vegetables, and drinks milk daily.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: African-American male child in no apparent discomfort, normal build and appearance.

Height: 160 cm (92nd percentile), Weight: 40 kgs (47th percentile)

Vital signs:
Temperature: 37° C
Pulse: 80 beats/min
BP: 105/66 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min

Skin: No lesions or abnormal markings.

HEENT: Moist mucous membranes, normal dentition, no caries. Eye examination and vision normal bilaterally. Hearing grossly normal.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No chest deformity.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen soft, nontender, nondistended.

Genitourinary: Normal male genitalia Tanner Stage 3, testes descended bilaterally.

Musculoskeletal: Back has mild paraspinous tenderness bilaterally in the thoracic region. When patient bends forward at the waist with his arms hanging and palms together, his shoulders are not level and his scapulae appear asymmetric. Palpation of the spinous processes show slight right thoracic and left lumbar curvature. There is no leg-length discrepancy, and iliac crests are symmetrical. Extremities have full range of motion, no visible or palpable deformities or tenderness of extremities or joints.

Neurologic: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Normal patellar relaxes 2+ bilaterally, 5/5 motor strength in bilateral upper and lower extremities. Normal gait. No clonus. No strictures or rigidity in the extremities.

Mental status: Appropriate affect and behavior.

Results of appropriate testing return and show the following results:

X-ray of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine:

No bony lesions noted. No signs of sacroiliitis. Scoliosis is present with right thoracic deviation and left lumbar deviation, Cobb angle 11°.

Joint hypermobility: Absent

Age: 12 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Intermittent mild upper back pain and stiffness for about a year, with findings of scoliosis on exam and X-ray.  
Analysis: The patient presents with mild thoracic back pain and stiffness without red flags. Physical exam reveals thoracic paraspinous tenderness, shoulder asymmetry on forward bend, and slight right thoracic and left lumbar curvature. X-ray confirms scoliosis with right thoracic and left lumbar deviation, Cobb angle 11°. No bony lesions, no sacroiliitis, no leg-length discrepancy. The clinical picture is consistent with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) given age, absence of neurological symptoms, normal neurological exam, and no other systemic findings. Differential considerations include postural asymmetry, leg-length discrepancy (excluded), neuromuscular scoliosis (no neurological findings), congenital scoliosis (no bony anomalies on X-ray), and other causes of back pain such as infection or tumor (excluded by absence of fever, weight loss, night pain, and normal X-ray). The Cobb angle of 11° is mild, and the patient is asymptomatic functionally. Given Tanner stage 3, he is still growing, so progression is possible and monitoring is warranted.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  
Conclusion: Mild adolescent idiopathic scoliosis with Cobb angle 11°, no evidence of underlying pathology, and no functional impairment. The patient is otherwise healthy.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics  
Recommendations: Refer to pediatric orthopedics for evaluation and management of scoliosis. Educate the patient and family about the natural history of AIS and the importance of monitoring for progression, especially during growth. Recommend repeat clinical examination and possibly repeat spine X-ray in 6–12 months or as advised by the orthopedic specialist. Encourage normal physical activity and sports without restrictions. Advise to seek medical attention if pain worsens, becomes nocturnal, or if new neurological symptoms (numbness, weakness, bowel/bladder changes) develop. Address the mild back pain with reassurance and over-the-counter analgesics if needed, but note that pain is not typical for AIS and if it persists or worsens, further evaluation may be needed.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 19  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: High fever, diffuse sunburn-like rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, progressive lightheadedness, and a retained menstrual tampon for ~3 days.  
Analysis: The clinical picture is highly consistent with toxic shock syndrome (TSS) due to Staphylococcus aureus (or Streptococcus pyogenes) toxin production. Strong supporting facts: fever (40.2°C), hypotension (BP 72/40), diffuse erythematous rash involving palms and soles, mucous membrane hyperemia, and multi-organ dysfunction (thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury with creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, elevated transaminases and CK). The retained tampon is the classic precipitating factor. Differential considerations include other causes of sepsis (e.g., gram-negative bacteremia, meningococcemia), Kawasaki disease, and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, but the tampon use and clinical constellation make TSS the most likely diagnosis.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures (already drawn), serum lactate, coagulation panel (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer), blood gas, urine output monitoring, and serial renal/hepatic function tests.  
Conclusion: This is a life-threatening case of menstrual toxic shock syndrome with septic shock and multi-organ dysfunction, requiring immediate aggressive management.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease  
Recommendations: Continue empiric clindamycin (to suppress toxin production) and vancomycin (for MRSA coverage). Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids (e.g., 30 mL/kg bolus) and vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) to maintain mean arterial pressure ≥65 mmHg. Remove any remaining foreign material (tampon already removed). Consider adding intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) if refractory shock or severe organ failure. Monitor for complications: acute respiratory distress syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and renal failure. Provide supportive care in an intensive care unit setting.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 32-year-old male singer presents with a hoarse voice that has persisted for 3 days following an intense concert performance. He reports mild sore throat and throat dryness but denies dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, fever, or hemoptysis. He is a non-smoker and does not consume alcohol regularly. He has no history of GERD or thyroid disease. On examination, he is afebrile. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without exudates or lesions. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His voice is notably hoarse and breathy. Respiratory effort is normal with no stridor or wheezing on auscultation.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 32
Sex: Male
Complaint: Hoarse, breathy voice persisting for 3 days after an intense concert performance, accompanied by mild sore throat and throat dryness.
Analysis: The patient is a young, otherwise healthy male singer with acute-onset hoarseness following intense vocal exertion. The breathy quality of the voice suggests vocal fold edema or strain. Key supporting facts include the clear temporal relationship to vocal overuse, absence of fever, dysphagia, stridor, dyspnea, or hemoptysis, and a benign oropharyngeal exam with only mild erythema and no exudates or lymphadenopathy. These findings point toward acute laryngitis or vocal fold strain rather than an infectious, neoplastic, or airway-threatening process. Differential considerations include acute viral laryngitis, vocal fold hemorrhage, or early vocal fold nodules; however, the lack of smoking, GERD, or systemic symptoms makes irritant or reflux etiologies less likely. The absence of respiratory distress and normal auscultation effectively rules out significant airway compromise.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Flexible laryngoscopy to evaluate the vocal folds for edema, hemorrhage, or lesions (recommended if symptoms persist or for professional voice assessment).
Conclusion: Acute laryngitis/vocal fold strain secondary to intense vocal use in a healthy young singer, with no evidence of airway compromise, infection, or serious underlying pathology.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)
Recommendations: Advise absolute voice rest for 24–48 hours, including avoidance of singing, whispering, and throat clearing. Maintain adequate hydration and use humidified air to soothe the throat. Warm salt water gargles may relieve mild sore throat. Avoid irritants such as smoke. If hoarseness persists beyond 2 weeks, worsens, or is accompanied by new symptoms (e.g., pain, dysphagia, or respiratory difficulty), refer for laryngoscopy and further ENT evaluation. The patient may resume singing only after the voice returns to normal.
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents after 8 hours of progressive wheezing and respiratory distress despite using his albuterol inhaler every 20 minutes at home. He has a history of moderate persistent asthma with two prior ICU admissions. He recently had an upper respiratory infection. On examination, he is sitting upright, using accessory muscles, and speaking in single words only. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 152, RR 42, BP 100/65, SpO2 87% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals markedly diminished breath sounds bilaterally with minimal wheezing, suggesting severe air trapping. Peak flow is unobtainable due to patient fatigue. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, pCO2 55 mmHg.

Age: 6
Sex: Male
Complaint: Progressive wheezing and respiratory distress for 8 hours despite frequent albuterol use, with hypoxia and signs of severe air trapping.
Analysis: This is a severe acute asthma exacerbation in a child with moderate persistent asthma and two prior ICU admissions. Key findings include marked tachypnea (RR 42), tachycardia (HR 152), hypoxia (SpO2 87% on room air), accessory muscle use, inability to speak in full sentences, and markedly diminished breath sounds with minimal wheezing ("silent chest") indicating severe air trapping. The venous blood gas shows respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28, pCO2 55 mmHg), which is a critical warning sign of impending respiratory failure, as pCO2 is elevated rather than low in a fatiguing patient. Peak flow is unobtainable due to fatigue. Differential considerations include severe asthma exacerbation with impending respiratory failure, and less likely pneumothorax, pneumonia, or foreign body aspiration, though the history strongly supports asthma.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous pulse oximetry, chest X-ray (to rule out pneumothorax, pneumonia, or complications), repeat arterial or venous blood gas, ECG and serum electrolytes (including potassium and glucose, given beta-agonist therapy), and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring.
Conclusion: Severe acute asthma exacerbation with impending respiratory failure, evidenced by respiratory acidosis, elevated pCO2, diminished breath sounds, and clinical fatigue despite aggressive home bronchodilator use.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Initiate immediate high-flow oxygen to maintain SpO2 > 92%. Administer continuous nebulized albuterol and ipratropium bromide, and give systemic corticosteroids (e.g., oral or IV methylprednisolone) promptly. Consider IV magnesium sulfate. Obtain a chest X-ray to exclude pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum. Prepare for escalation to noninvasive ventilation or intubation given the elevated pCO2 and fatigue. Transfer to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) given the history of two prior ICU admissions and current severity. Reassess frequently for deterioration, and monitor for hypokalemia and hyperglycemia from beta-agonist therapy.
Notes: The elevated pCO2 with respiratory acidosis in the setting of a "silent chest" is a red flag for impending respiratory arrest; do not delay escalation of care. Avoid sedatives that may depress respiratory drive.

Age: 53
Sex: Female
Complaint: Intermittent palpitations (sensation of irregular and racing heartbeats) accompanied by fatigue over the past 2 months.
Analysis: The patient presents with intermittent palpitations lasting 10 minutes to several hours, occurring once or twice weekly and resolving spontaneously. She denies chest pain, dyspnea, light-headedness, and syncope, and is active without exertional symptoms. She has well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Physical examination is reassuring: regular rate and rhythm at 58 bpm, normal S1/S2, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, no JVD, and clear lungs. Given the intermittent nature of symptoms and a normal resting exam, the main differential includes paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, supraventricular tachycardia, and premature atrial or ventricular beats. The absence of concerning symptoms (syncope, chest pain, dyspnea) and stable hemodynamics make this non-emergent. Ambulatory ECG monitoring is needed to capture the arrhythmia, and thyroid dysfunction should be excluded as a reversible cause of palpitations.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: 12-lead ECG, ambulatory cardiac monitoring (Holter monitor or event monitor), thyroid function tests (TSH), basic metabolic panel, complete blood count.
Conclusion: A 53-year-old woman with intermittent palpitations and fatigue, hemodynamically stable with a reassuring physical exam, likely due to a paroxysmal arrhythmia. Requires outpatient evaluation with ambulatory ECG monitoring to establish the diagnosis.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology

baseline_protocol:
Age: 72  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Increased sputum production with color change to yellow-green and mild worsening of baseline dyspnea over 5 days.  
Analysis: The patient has known COPD (GOLD stage II) and a 40-pack-year smoking history. He presents with a 5-day history of increased sputum production, purulent sputum (yellow-green), and mild worsening dyspnea. He denies fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, or significant increase in cough frequency. Vital signs are stable (temperature 98.6°F, HR 82, BP 134/78, RR 20, SpO2 93% on room air, baseline 94-95%). Examination shows mild bilateral expiratory wheezing without accessory muscle use, and he speaks in full sentences comfortably. These findings are consistent with a mild to moderate acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD). The purulent sputum suggests an infectious trigger. Differential considerations include pneumonia (unlikely given no fever, no focal findings, and stable vitals), congestive heart failure (no crackles, orthopnea, or edema), and pulmonary embolism (no chest pain or hemoptysis). The absence of respiratory failure (no accessory muscle use, normal mental status, near-baseline oxygen saturation) indicates a non-severe exacerbation.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest X-ray (to rule out pneumonia), sputum culture (given purulent sputum), and complete blood count (to assess for leukocytosis).  
Conclusion: Acute exacerbation of COPD (mild to moderate) with purulent sputum, without evidence of respiratory failure or pneumonia.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  
Recommendations: Initiate outpatient management. Prescribe a short course of oral corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days) to reduce airway inflammation. Start antibiotics for purulent sputum (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate or doxycycline) for 5-7 days. Increase use of short-acting bronchodilator (albuterol) as needed, and ensure proper inhaler technique. Continue maintenance therapy with tiotropium. Monitor oxygen saturation; if it drops below 90% or symptoms worsen, seek urgent care. Advise smoking cessation and provide counseling. Schedule follow-up in 48-72 hours to reassess response to treatment.

Vignette:
A 72-year-old woman presents with generalized dry, itchy skin that has been worsening over the past several weeks as winter has progressed. She reports the itching is worst on her shins and forearms. She bathes daily in hot water and uses regular bar soap. She denies any new medications, rash, jaundice, or unintentional weight loss. On examination, the skin on the extremities is diffusely dry with fine scaling and superficial cracking. There are no excoriations, erythematous plaques, or papules. Skin turgor is appropriate for age. No jaundice or lymphadenopathy is noted.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 72
Sex: Female
Complaint: Generalized dry, itchy skin worsening over several weeks, worst on shins and forearms.
Analysis: The presentation is most consistent with xerosis cutis (winter itch / asteatotic eczema). Strongest supporting facts: elderly patient, onset during winter, daily hot water bathing with regular bar soap (both strip skin lipids and worsen dryness), and examination showing diffusely dry skin with fine scaling and superficial cracking on the extremities without excoriations, erythematous plaques, or papules. The absence of rash, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, new medications, and unintentional weight loss argues against inflammatory dermatoses (e.g., atopic or contact dermatitis), infestations (e.g., scabies), or systemic causes of pruritus (e.g., cholestasis, renal failure, thyroid disease, malignancy). Skin turgor appropriate for age and lack of systemic signs further support a benign, localized skin-barrier problem.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (clinical diagnosis; no additional testing needed at this stage).
Conclusion: Xerosis cutis (winter itch / asteatotic eczema) secondary to cold, dry winter air and irritant bathing habits (hot water and bar soap) in an elderly patient.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology
Recommendations: Discontinue hot water bathing and regular bar soap; bathe with lukewarm water and a mild, fragrance-free cleanser. Apply a thick emollient or moisturizer (e.g., petrolatum-based or ceramide-containing cream) immediately after bathing and multiple times daily, especially on the shins and forearms. Use a humidifier in the home to counteract dry winter air. Avoid harsh soaps, excessive scrubbing, and tight or woolen clothing. If itching persists despite these measures, consider a short course of low-potency topical corticosteroid or reevaluate for systemic causes of pruritus.
Notes: If symptoms do not improve with conservative skin care or if new rash, weight loss, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy develops, further workup for systemic disease is warranted.

Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.

- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 17
Sex: Female
Complaint: Intentional acetaminophen overdose (approximately 25 g) 12 hours prior, now with nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
Analysis: The patient presents with acute acetaminophen toxicity following a large intentional ingestion (25 g, far exceeding the hepatotoxic threshold). The acetaminophen level of 180 mcg/mL at 12 hours is well above the treatment line on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, confirming toxicity. Elevated AST (1,240 U/L) and ALT (1,086 U/L), INR 1.8, and total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL indicate early hepatotoxicity. The pH of 7.34 and lactate of 2.8 mmol/L are concerning but do not yet meet criteria for fulminant hepatic failure (pH <7.30, INR >6.5, or creatinine >3.4). Differential considerations include other causes of acute hepatitis (viral, ischemic), but the history and laboratory findings strongly support acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity. The psychiatric context (intentional ingestion after a breakup) is a critical component requiring concurrent mental health management.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serial liver function tests (AST, ALT), INR/PT, renal function (creatinine), arterial blood gas, lactate, glucose, and repeat acetaminophen levels; monitoring for hepatic encephalopathy; liver ultrasound may be considered.
Conclusion: Acute acetaminophen overdose with early hepatotoxicity (elevated transaminases, INR, and bilirubin) in the setting of a suicidal gesture. N-acetylcysteine therapy has been appropriately initiated. The patient requires emergent care and close monitoring for progression to fulminant hepatic failure.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Continue N-acetylcysteine infusion per protocol. Monitor serial AST/ALT, INR, bilirubin, creatinine, pH, and lactate. Assess for hepatic encephalopathy and hypoglycemia. Consider transfer to a liver transplant center if signs of fulminant hepatic failure develop (pH <7.30, INR >6.5, creatinine >3.4, or encephalopathy). Provide psychiatric evaluation and suicide risk assessment, and ensure social work involvement. Maintain poison control consultation. Avoid additional hepatotoxic agents.
Notes: The patient is at high risk for progression to acute liver failure; NAC started at 12 hours post-ingestion remains beneficial but requires close follow-up. Monitor for psychiatric safety throughout hospitalization.

He has a history of choledocholithiasis with a prior ERCP and sphincterotomy 5 years ago. On examination, he appears jaundiced and acutely ill with intermittent rigors. Vignette:
A 70-year-old man presents with 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive yellowing of his skin and eyes. He has a history of choledocholithiasis with a prior ERCP and sphincterotomy 5 years ago. On examination, he appears jaundiced and acutely ill with intermittent rigors. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 88/52, SpO2 96%. Abdominal examination reveals significant right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign. Scleral icterus is prominent. Labs: WBC 22,600/mcL with 15% bands, total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, ALP 482 U/L, AST 188 U/L, ALT 162 U/L, lipase normal, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures are drawn. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows common bile duct dilation to 14 mm with a shadowing stone in the distal CBD and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 70
Sex: Male
Complaint: Right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive jaundice for 18 hours.
Analysis: The patient presents with Charcot's triad (right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and jaundice) plus hypotension (BP 88/52) and elevated lactate (4.1 mmol/L), consistent with Reynolds' pentad and severe acute cholangitis with septic shock. Supporting findings include leukocytosis with left shift (WBC 22,600, 15% bands), obstructive liver profile (total bilirubin 8.4, direct 6.8, ALP 482), and ultrasound showing CBD dilation to 14 mm with a distal shadowing stone and intrahepatic ductal dilation. Prior ERCP/sphincterotomy increases risk of recurrent choledocholithiasis. Differential considerations include acute cholecystitis (positive Murphy sign, but CBD stone and cholestasis favor cholangitis), hepatic abscess, and biliary obstruction from malignancy; normal lipase excludes acute pancreatitis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures (already drawn), complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation panel, blood gas, and urgent ERCP with biliary drainage capability; bedside ultrasound already performed.
Conclusion: Severe acute cholangitis (Tokyo grade III) with septic shock secondary to distal common bile duct stone obstruction, requiring emergent biliary decompression and resuscitative support.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: Initiate immediate aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) for persistent hypotension; start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) after blood cultures; perform urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction or biliary stent placement for drainage; admit to intensive care unit for hemodynamic monitoring; correct any coagulopathy and monitor renal function and lactate; reassess for signs of perforation or abscess.
Notes: None

baseline_protocol:
Age: 3 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Low-grade fever (37.8°C) with small blisters on the hands and feet and a few sores inside the mouth since this morning.
Analysis: The combination of low-grade fever, vesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and dorsal hands, and shallow oral ulcers in a young child with known daycare exposure to similar symptoms is highly characteristic of Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD), a common, typically self-limiting enteroviral infection (most often Coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71). The child is alert, playful, and well-hydrated, and is eating and drinking well, indicating a mild course. Main differential considerations include herpangina (oral ulcers without extremity rash), other viral exanthems, and contact dermatitis, but the classic distribution and daycare exposure strongly support HFMD.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (clinical diagnosis; no laboratory or imaging studies are needed in this typical, mild presentation).
Conclusion: Mild, self-limiting Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) in a well-appearing, well-hydrated 3-year-old child.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Provide supportive care at home: ensure adequate fluid intake to maintain hydration; use antipyretics (e.g., acetaminophen or ibuprofen) for fever or discomfort; offer soft, cool, bland foods and avoid acidic, salty, or spicy items that may irritate oral ulcers. Keep the child home from daycare until fever has resolved and vesicles have dried (typically 5–7 days). Practice good hand hygiene and avoid sharing utensils to prevent spread. Advise the mother to return for evaluation if the child develops high fever, lethargy, poor oral intake with signs of dehydration (decreased urination, dry mouth, no tears), or any neurological symptoms (e.g., weakness, seizures, altered mental status).
Notes: HFMD is highly contagious and spreads easily in daycare settings; rare complications include viral meningitis or encephalitis, particularly with enterovirus 71, so parents should be counseled on warning signs. No antibiotics or antiviral therapy are indicated.

Vignette:
A 68-yr-old woman comes to the office with her daughter because of a 4-mo history of gradually
increasing lethargy and worsening memory. Her daughter is concerned because the mother has
stopped remembering whether she has taken her regular medications. The daughter is worried
that her mother might not be safe to live on her own. Prior to 4 mo ago, the woman had been
very busy with community activities, which she has since stopped, and her daughter had not
noticed any memory difficulties. The daughter is not aware of any recent illnesses or injuries.
Review of Systems:
General: The patient says she feels tired all the time and is usually cold even now during the
summer. She has a poor appetite but has gained 5 kg in weight in the preceding 4 mo despite
decreased appetite. No fever, chills, headache, or body aches.

Skin: Her skin has become dry, and her hair is now coarse and sparse. No rash or itching.

HEENT: She reports fullness in her throat, and her daughter has noticed that her mother's
voice has become hoarse and her face appears puffy, particularly around the eyes. No difficulty
swallowing.

Pulmonary: The patient reports new exertional shortness of breath and needing to pause after
climbing 1/2 flight of stairs. No cough or wheezing.

Cardiovascular: She used to have occasional palpitations before but has had none for the last 2
mo. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Gastrointestinal: The patient's bowel movements have decreased from daily to once every 3
to 4 days when using laxatives. She does not have any abdominal pain or vomiting. Her
appetite is decreased.

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Musculoskeletal: Her ankles and lower legs are more swollen than they used to be. She reports
fatigue and leg weakness when climbing stairs or getting up from a chair.

Neurologic: She has become slower at performing daily activities, and extra effort is required.
Her daughter has noticed that her mother has trouble remembering recent events, such as
whether she has taken her medications. She denies having focal weakness or sensory
abnormalities, tremor, or visual symptoms.

Psychiatric: Her mood is depressed and she often stays in bed, not going out of the house for

Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.

Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case

- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.

Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. - If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. baseline_protocol:
Age: 68  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: 4-month history of progressive lethargy, worsening memory, cold intolerance, weight gain despite poor appetite, dry skin, hoarseness, periorbital edema, constipation, leg swelling, and depressed mood.  
Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for severe primary hypothyroidism. Supporting findings include markedly elevated TSH (88 microIU/mL), low free T4 (0.4 ng/dL) and free T3 (0.8 pg/mL), and positive serum TPO antibodies (258 IU/mL), confirming autoimmune (Hashimoto’s) thyroiditis. Systemic manifestations are evident: cognitive slowing, bradycardia (56 bpm, irregular due to known AF), cold intolerance, weight gain, dry coarse skin and hair, periorbital edema, hoarse voice, constipation, ankle edema, proximal muscle weakness, delayed reflexes, and depression. Laboratory abnormalities include mild hyponatremia (135 mEq/L) and normocytic anemia (Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 88 fL). Chest x-ray shows mild fluid overload and cardiomegaly, consistent with heart failure exacerbation. Differential considerations include other causes of cognitive decline (e.g., dementia, depression) and heart failure, but the thyroid profile is diagnostic. The patient’s history of AF and prior heart failure, along with current crackles and edema, indicate that hypothyroidism is contributing to cardiovascular decompensation.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (diagnosis is established; further testing is not needed for immediate management).  
Conclusion: Severe primary hypothyroidism (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis) with multisystem involvement, including cognitive impairment, heart failure exacerbation, anemia, and hyponatremia. The patient requires thyroid hormone replacement with careful cardiovascular and anticoagulation monitoring.  
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  
Recommendations: Initiate levothyroxine at a low dose (e.g., 25–50 mcg daily) with gradual titration, given the patient’s age and cardiac history. Monitor TSH and free T4 every 6–8 weeks. Because thyroid hormone replacement can increase warfarin sensitivity, monitor INR closely and adjust warfarin dose as needed. Continue current cardiac medications (bisoprolol, ramipril, furosemide) but reassess furosemide dose as edema improves. Expect cognitive, mood, and physical symptoms to improve with euthyroidism. Address anemia and hyponatremia if they persist after thyroid normalization. Provide education on medication adherence and involve the daughter in care planning. Consider cardiology referral for ongoing AF and heart failure management. Evaluate the right-sided carpal tunnel syndrome (positive Tinel’s sign) if symptoms persist after thyroid treatment.  
Notes: Use caution with levothyroxine in elderly patients with cardiac disease—start low and titrate slowly. The bradycardia and irregular pulse are consistent with AF and hypothyroidism. Hyponatremia and anemia are likely secondary to hypothyroidism and should improve with replacement.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 61
Sex: Female
Complaint: Four days of cough productive of yellow sputum, preceded by rhinorrhea, with initial fevers up to 101°F that have resolved.
Analysis: The patient presents with an acute productive cough and rhinorrhea following a typical viral upper respiratory tract infection course. Fevers have resolved, and she is currently afebrile with normal vital signs and a normal physical examination. Her only comorbidity is hypercholesterolemia treated with atorvastatin, and she has no drug allergies. The most likely diagnosis is acute bronchitis of viral etiology, given the self-limited course, resolution of fever, and normal exam. Differential considerations include a common cold with bronchitis, influenza, or a mild bacterial bronchitis; however, the absence of fever, normal vital signs, and normal lung exam make pneumonia unlikely. Antibiotics are not indicated for acute bronchitis in an otherwise healthy patient without evidence of pneumonia.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (no additional testing indicated given normal vital signs, normal physical exam, and typical viral presentation).
Conclusion: Acute bronchitis, likely viral, in a healthy 61-year-old woman with a resolving clinical course and no signs of pneumonia or bacterial superinfection.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine
Recommendations: Provide symptomatic management including adequate hydration, rest, and over-the-counter cough suppressants or expectorants as needed for symptom relief. Reassure the patient that the cough may persist for up to 2-3 weeks. Advise against antibiotics, as they are not indicated for acute bronchitis without evidence of bacterial infection. Instruct the patient to return or seek care if she develops worsening symptoms, recurrence of high fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, hemoptysis, or if symptoms fail to improve within 2-3 weeks. Continue atorvastatin as prescribed.

Vignette:
A 9-month-old male infant is brought in by his parents after 8 hours of episodic inconsolable crying during which he draws his legs up to his abdomen, alternating with periods of lethargy. The parents report two episodes of vomiting and one bowel movement containing dark red mucus-like material. He had a viral upper respiratory infection last week. On examination, during a pain-free interval, the infant is pale and lethargic. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 168, RR 36, BP 80/52. Abdomen is mildly distended with a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. The right lower quadrant feels empty (Dance sign). Rectal exam reveals currant jelly stool on the examining finger. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a target sign (doughnut sign) in the right upper quadrant, confirming ileocolic intussusception, with no evidence of perforation or peritonitis. Air enema reduction is arranged.
baseline_protocol:

Sex: Male
Complaint: Episodic inconsolable crying with legs drawn up to the abdomen, alternating with lethargy, two episodes of vomiting, and one bowel movement with dark red mucus-like material.
Analysis: The infant presents with classic features of ileocolic intussusception: episodic colicky abdominal pain (crying with legs drawn up), vomiting, currant jelly stool on rectal exam, a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant, and an empty right lower quadrant (Dance sign). The abdominal ultrasound confirms the diagnosis with a target/doughnut sign. There is no evidence of perforation or peritonitis. The recent viral upper respiratory infection is a known predisposing factor. The vital signs (tachycardia, mild tachypnea) and lethargy suggest early compromise but no overt shock or peritonitis. Main differential considerations include gastroenteritis, volvulus, Meckel diverticulum, and other causes of bowel obstruction or bleeding, but the imaging findings are diagnostic.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None (diagnosis confirmed by ultrasound; air enema reduction equipment is arranged for therapeutic intervention).
Conclusion: Ileocolic intussusception in a 9-month-old infant, confirmed by ultrasound, without perforation or peritonitis, requiring urgent air enema reduction.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Proceed with air enema reduction under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance as arranged. Obtain IV access and provide fluid resuscitation given tachycardia and lethargy. Monitor closely during and after reduction for signs of perforation (e.g., sudden deterioration, abdominal distension, peritonitis) or failed reduction. If air enema reduction is unsuccessful or contraindicated, consult pediatric surgery for operative reduction. Observe the infant after successful reduction for recurrence, and monitor vital signs, hydration status, and return of normal bowel function. Address the additional consideration of the recent viral upper respiratory infection as a potential trigger, but no specific antiviral therapy is indicated.
Notes: Watch for signs of perforation or peritonitis during air enema reduction; recurrence of intussusception is possible and warrants parental education on warning signs.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 70
Sex: Male
Complaint: 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency with mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever (100.4°F).
Analysis: The patient presents with classic lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency) accompanied by suprapubic tenderness and low-grade fever. Urinalysis showing pyuria and positive nitrites strongly supports a bacterial urinary tract infection. His history of BPH is a significant risk factor for complicated UTI and urinary stasis. The absence of flank pain, rigors, and guarding argues against pyelonephritis or an acute surgical abdomen. The nontender, enlarged prostate on DRE, combined with fever, raises the possibility of acute bacterial prostatitis. The patient is hemodynamically stable (normal BP and HR, no acute distress), indicating a non-severe presentation. Main differential considerations include acute cystitis, acute bacterial prostatitis, and complicated UTI secondary to BPH.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urine culture and sensitivity (before initiating antibiotics); consider serum complete blood count and creatinine to assess for systemic involvement and baseline renal function.
Conclusion: Acute bacterial urinary tract infection (cystitis) with possible acute bacterial prostatitis in the setting of benign prostatic hyperplasia; patient is clinically stable with no signs of sepsis or upper tract involvement.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Urology
Recommendations: Initiate empirical oral antibiotics appropriate for complicated UTI/prostatitis (e.g., a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole based on local resistance patterns), after obtaining a urine culture. Advise adequate hydration and symptomatic relief (e.g., urinary analgesic such as phenazopyridine if needed). Continue tamsulosin for BPH. Arrange outpatient follow-up within 48–72 hours to review culture results and clinical response. If fever persists, symptoms worsen, or signs of urinary obstruction develop, reassess promptly and consider imaging (e.g., renal/bladder ultrasound) to evaluate for obstruction or abscess. Counsel the patient to seek urgent care for flank pain, rigors, vomiting, or inability to void.
Notes: The presence of fever in a male with BPH should prompt consideration of acute bacterial prostatitis, which typically requires a longer course of antibiotics (e.g., 2–4 weeks) compared to simple cystitis; confirm with culture and adjust therapy accordingly.

Vignette:
A 66-year-old woman presents with 2 days of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain, and intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent. She has not passed flatus or had a bowel movement for 36 hours. Her surgical history includes an open appendectomy 30 years ago and a total abdominal hysterectomy 15 years ago. On examination, she appears dehydrated and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 110, RR 20, BP 108/68, SpO2 97%. Abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. There is diffuse tenderness, greatest in the periumbilical region, with mild involuntary guarding. Labs: WBC 14,800/mcL, BUN 42, creatinine 1.6, lactate 3.1 mmol/L. CT abdomen demonstrates dilated small bowel loops up to 5.2 cm with a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant with a small bowel feces sign and possible closed-loop configuration.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 66
Sex: Female
Complaint: Progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain, intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent, and absence of flatus or bowel movement for 36 hours.
Analysis: The patient presents with clinical and radiographic features of a high-grade small bowel obstruction (SBO). Strong supporting facts include prior abdominal surgeries (open appendectomy and total abdominal hysterectomy) predisposing to adhesive disease; feculent vomiting and 36 hours without flatus or stool indicating a complete/advanced obstruction; and CT findings of dilated small bowel loops (5.2 cm), a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant, a small bowel feces sign, and a possible closed-loop configuration. Elevated lactate (3.1 mmol/L), leukocytosis (WBC 14,800), tachycardia, and mild involuntary guarding raise concern for bowel ischemia or strangulation. Main differential considerations include adhesive small bowel obstruction (most likely), closed-loop obstruction with strangulation, internal hernia, volvulus, and incarcerated hernia; less likely are malignancy or inflammatory stricture. The possible closed-loop configuration with metabolic derangements makes this a surgical emergency.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None additional imaging required (CT already performed); urgent surgical consultation, repeat lactate, arterial blood gas, and type and crossmatch are required.
Conclusion: High-grade small bowel obstruction with a possible closed-loop configuration and signs concerning for strangulation (elevated lactate, leukocytosis, feculent vomiting) in a patient with prior abdominal surgeries. This constitutes a surgical emergency requiring urgent operative intervention.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Urgent general surgery consultation for emergent laparotomy/exploration given the suspected closed-loop/strangulated obstruction. Initiate aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and correct electrolyte abnormalities. Place a nasogastric tube for gastric decompression. Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics. Monitor urine output and perform serial abdominal examinations and serial lactate measurements. Do not delay surgery for a possible closed-loop obstruction; conservative (non-operative) management is contraindicated in this setting.
Notes: The possible closed-loop configuration and elevated lactate are red flags for strangulation and mandate urgent operative intervention rather than conservative management.

Vignette:
A 40-year-old male construction worker is extricated by rescue crews after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall at a building site for approximately 4 hours. Both lower extremities were pinned. Upon extrication, he is alert and reports severe pain in both legs and a sensation of numbness. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, both lower extremities are markedly swollen, tense, and ecchymotic from the thighs to the ankles. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 118, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 95%. Pedal pulses are weak bilaterally. Sensation is diminished throughout both legs. He reports dark brown urine since a Foley catheter was placed in the field, with only 50 mL output over the past 2 hours. Labs drawn immediately: potassium 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, CK 124,000 U/L, phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL, calcium 6.2 mg/dL, uric acid 14.2 mg/dL, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation at 1.5 L/hr with sodium bicarbonate supplementation is initiated, along with continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection.

Age: 40
Sex: Male
Complaint: Severe pain and numbness in both legs after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall for 4 hours; dark brown urine with markedly reduced urine output (50 mL over 2 hours).
Analysis: The patient presents with classic crush syndrome following prolonged compression of both lower extremities. Key supporting findings include massive rhabdomyolysis (CK 124,000 U/L, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL), acute kidney injury (creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, oliguria), life-threatening hyperkalemia (potassium 6.8 mEq/L with peaked T waves on ECG), metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L), hyperphosphatemia (7.6 mg/dL), hypocalcemia (6.2 mg/dL), and hyperuricemia (14.2 mg/dL). Dark brown urine indicates myoglobinuria. Hypotension (BP 96/62) and tachycardia (HR 118) reflect hypovolemia and systemic toxicity. Differential considerations include compartment syndrome of the lower extremities (tense, swollen limbs with weak pulses and diminished sensation), acute tubular necrosis from pigment nephropathy, and hyperkalemic cardiac arrhythmia. This is a life-threatening, time-critical emergency.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring (ongoing); serial serum potassium, CK, creatinine, calcium, phosphorus, and arterial blood gas; urine output monitoring with Foley catheter; compartment pressure measurement of both lower extremities; serial ECG.
Conclusion: Crush syndrome complicated by severe rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, life-threatening hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis requiring immediate aggressive resuscitation and cardiac protection.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Continue aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation (1.5 L/hr) with sodium bicarbonate to maintain urine output and alkalinize urine; continue IV calcium gluconate for cardiac protection against hyperkalemia; add insulin with dextrose and consider beta-agonists to shift potassium intracellularly; monitor for refractory hyperkalemia, fluid overload, or uremia and initiate renal replacement therapy (hemodialysis) if indicated; assess both lower extremities for compartment syndrome with compartment pressure measurement and consult orthopedics for possible fasciotomy; monitor urine output closely and adjust fluids to avoid volume overload; correct hypocalcemia only if symptomatic (to avoid calcium-phosphate precipitation); treat hyperuricemia as needed; provide analgesia and tetanus prophylaxis as appropriate.
Notes: Hypocalcemia should not be aggressively corrected unless symptomatic, as it may worsen calcium-phosphate precipitation in the setting of hyperphosphatemia. Compartment syndrome must be actively monitored and may require urgent fasciotomy. Continuous cardiac monitoring is essential given the risk of hyperkalemic arrhythmias.

baseline_protocol:
Age: 47
Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden onset thunderclap headache (worst of life, maximal within seconds) during straining, with vomiting, brief loss of consciousness, photophobia, irritability, and stiff neck.
Analysis: The presentation of a thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds, accompanied by vomiting, transient loss of consciousness, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity, strongly suggests acute subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Non-contrast CT confirms diffuse SAH in the basal cisterns, and CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm as the likely bleeding source. The Hunt and Hess grade III (irritable, mild focal deficit) indicates moderate clinical severity. Differential considerations include other causes of thunderclap headache (e.g., cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, pituitary apoplexy, cervical artery dissection), but the imaging findings establish aneurysmal SAH as the diagnosis. The patient's smoking history is a significant risk factor for aneurysm formation and rupture.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) for detailed aneurysm characterization and treatment planning; laboratory studies (CBC, coagulation profile, electrolytes, renal function); ECG; chest X-ray; serial transcranial Doppler for vasospasm surveillance.
Conclusion: Ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm causing diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage, Hunt and Hess grade III, in a 47-year-old female smoker; a life-threatening neurosurgical emergency with high risk of rebleeding and vasospasm.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Immediate neurosurgical consultation for urgent aneurysm securing (surgical clipping or endovascular coiling). Initiate blood pressure control to reduce rebleeding risk (target systolic <160 mm Hg, e.g., nicardipine or labetalol). Administer oral nimodipine (60 mg every 4 hours) for vasospasm prophylaxis. Provide analgesia, antiemetics, and stool softeners to avoid straining. Maintain strict bed rest with head elevation; monitor neurological status and vital signs closely. Consider serial imaging for hydrocephalus and transcranial Doppler for vasospasm (peak risk days 4–14). Address smoking cessation counseling. Manage elevated BP (178/96) cautiously to avoid hypotension and maintain cerebral perfusion.
Notes: Hunt and Hess grade III carries significant morbidity/mortality; risk of early rebleeding is highest within the first 24–72 hours, and delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm is a major concern. Avoid lumbar puncture given confirmed SAH on CT. None

Vignette:
A 5-month-old baby boy presents with difficulty and delay in passing hard stools. His mother reports that he strains for several hours and may even miss a day, before passing stool with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper. He has recently been weaned from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula, which he had been reluctant to drink initially. The child is thriving and now feeding normally. There was no neonatal delay in defecation and no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension.

Age: 5 months
Sex: Male
Complaint: Difficulty and delay in passing hard stools, with prolonged straining, screaming, and occasional spots of fresh blood on stool or diaper, following weaning from breast milk to cow's milk formula.
Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with functional constipation in an infant, likely triggered by the recent transition from breast milk to cow's milk formula. Supporting facts include hard stools, prolonged straining, and fresh blood spots (suggesting anal fissures from passing hard stools). The absence of neonatal delay in defecation, excessive vomiting, or abdominal distension, along with normal thriving and feeding, argues against organic causes such as Hirschsprung's disease or intestinal obstruction. Cow's milk protein intolerance is a possible differential, but the child is thriving and feeding normally, making it less likely. The main differential considerations are functional constipation, anal fissure secondary to hard stool, and cow's milk protein allergy.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Physical examination including inspection of the perianal area for fissures and abdominal examination; no laboratory or imaging studies are immediately required.
Conclusion: Functional constipation in a thriving 5-month-old infant, temporally associated with weaning to cow's milk formula, complicated by minor anal fissures causing fresh blood spots.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: Reassure the mother that this is a common, manageable condition. Optimize feeding: consider continuing breastfeeding if possible, or ensure proper formula preparation and adequate fluid intake. If constipation persists, discuss switching to a formula with partially hydrolyzed protein or a lactose-reduced preparation, given the recent formula change. Manage hard stools with an age-appropriate intervention such as oral lactulose or a glycerin suppository, under pediatric guidance. Treat and prevent anal fissures with gentle perianal hygiene and barrier ointment. Advise the mother to monitor for red flags including poor weight gain, abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, or delayed passage of meconium, which would warrant urgent reassessment. Schedule a follow-up visit to confirm improvement.
Notes: None

Vignette:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of SOB of 30 minutes' duration. Initially, he felt faint but did not lose consciousness. He is complaining of left-sided chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration. He has no history of cardiopulmonary disease. A week ago he underwent a total left hip replacement and, following discharge, was on bed rest for 3 days due to poorly controlled pain. He subsequently noticed swelling in his left calf, which is tender on examination. His current vital signs reveal a fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C), heart rate 112 bpm, BP 95/65, and an O2 saturation on room air of 91%.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 65
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute onset shortness of breath (30 minutes), faintness without loss of consciousness, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, and left calf swelling with tenderness.
Analysis: The patient presents with acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and near-syncope in the setting of recent total left hip replacement, 3 days of postoperative bed rest, and a swollen, tender left calf—all classic risk factors and findings for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) with subsequent pulmonary embolism (PE). His vital signs show fever (38.0°C), tachycardia (112 bpm), hypotension (BP 95/65), and hypoxia (SpO2 91% on room air), indicating a hemodynamically significant PE. The pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, and hypotension strongly support acute PE as the leading diagnosis. Differential considerations include acute coronary syndrome, pneumonia, pneumothorax, and pericarditis, but the combination of recent surgery, immobilization, unilateral calf swelling, and acute pleuritic chest pain with hypoxia makes PE the most probable and dangerous diagnosis.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA), lower extremity venous Doppler ultrasound, ECG, chest X-ray, arterial blood gas, D-dimer (if CTPA not immediately available), troponin, BNP, and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring.
Conclusion: Acute pulmonary embolism, likely originating from a left lower extremity DVT following hip replacement and prolonged bed rest, presenting with hemodynamic compromise (hypotension, hypoxia, tachycardia) consistent with a massive or submassive PE requiring urgent intervention.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Initiate immediate stabilization: administer high-flow supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 ≥ 94%, establish IV access, and place the patient on continuous cardiac and blood pressure monitoring. Given hypotension (BP 95/65), provide cautious fluid resuscitation and consider vasopressor support if hypotension persists. Obtain urgent CTPA to confirm the diagnosis; if clinical suspicion is high and CTPA is delayed, start therapeutic anticoagulation (e.g., unfractionated heparin) provided there are no contraindications. Given hemodynamic instability, evaluate for thrombolysis or embolectomy if massive PE is confirmed. Perform lower extremity venous Doppler to confirm DVT. Admit to an intensive care unit and consult cardiology and pulmonology for ongoing management. Monitor for signs of right heart strain (ECG, troponin, BNP) and reassess oxygenation and hemodynamics frequently.
Notes: The fever is a recognized but non-specific finding in PE and should not delay diagnosis. Hypotension and hypoxia indicate a potentially life-threatening PE; avoid unnecessary delays in diagnostic imaging and anticoagulation. Consider bleeding risk from recent surgery when initiating thrombolytic therapy.

The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden onset of painful vaginal bleeding with severe constant abdominal pain at 34 weeks gestation, decreased fetal movement, signs of hemorrhagic shock, and fetal distress.
Analysis: The presentation is consistent with acute placental abruption with a "woody" firm, tender uterus, dark red vaginal bleeding, and fetal distress (baseline FHR 170 bpm, absent variability, repetitive late decelerations). Risk factors include chronic hypertension and prior placental abruption. The laboratory findings (low fibrinogen 142 mg/dL, elevated PT 14.8 s, D-dimer >20,000 ng/mL, thrombocytopenia 108,000/mcL, anemia 8.4 g/dL) indicate disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) secondary to the abruption. Differential considerations include placenta previa, uterine rupture, and vasa previa, but the woody uterus, coagulopathy, and fetal distress strongly favor placental abruption with DIC.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous maternal and fetal monitoring (already in place); repeat coagulation profile (fibrinogen, PT/INR, aPTT, D-dimer, platelets) and hemoglobin/hematocrit during resuscitation; type and crossmatch with ongoing blood product availability; point-of-care viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) if available; arterial blood gas for acid-base status; bedside ultrasound to confirm fetal viability and placental findings if time permits.
Conclusion: This is a severe placental abruption at 34 weeks gestation complicated by DIC and hemorrhagic shock, with evidence of fetal compromise. Emergent cesarean delivery is indicated, with aggressive maternal resuscitation and correction of coagulopathy.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology
Recommendations: Proceed immediately with emergent cesarean delivery with a multidisciplinary team (obstetrics, anesthesia, neonatology, hematology/blood bank). Continue aggressive transfusion with packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate (to correct fibrinogen), and platelets per massive transfusion protocol. Administer uterotonics (e.g., oxytocin, and consider methergine/carboprost if no contraindications) after delivery to reduce postpartum hemorrhage. Prepare for possible hysterectomy if bleeding is uncontrolled. Provide neonatal resuscitation team for the preterm infant. Transfer to ICU postoperatively for ongoing hemodynamic and coagulation monitoring. Address the DIC with serial labs and goal-directed correction of fibrinogen and platelets. Monitor for renal failure, Sheehan syndrome, and other complications of hypovolemic shock.

Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 30  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Severe pain, tearing, foreign body sensation, and photophobia in the left eye for 6 hours after a metal-grinding injury without eye protection; a 3 mm linear central corneal epithelial defect is present.  
Analysis: The patient sustained a traumatic corneal abrasion from a metallic foreign body strike. Fluorescein staining confirms a 3 mm linear central epithelial defect. The negative Seidel test rules out full-thickness corneal perforation (open globe). No retained foreign body is seen on slit lamp examination or lid eversion, and there is no hypopyon or hyphema, with a round reactive pupil. The main differentials include corneal abrasion (confirmed), retained corneal or intraocular foreign body (ruled out on slit lamp/lid eversion but high-velocity metal injury warrants consideration of intraocular foreign body), corneal laceration/ruptured globe (excluded by negative Seidel), and infectious keratitis (risk increased due to contact lens use, particularly Pseudomonas). The blurry vision is attributed to tearing rather than structural damage.  
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Dilated fundus examination to rule out posterior segment intraocular foreign body; orbital imaging (e.g., CT) if intraocular foreign body is suspected; corneal culture if signs of infection develop.  
Conclusion: Traumatic corneal abrasion of the left eye with no retained foreign body, no corneal perforation, and no evidence of intraocular infection or inflammation. Requires prompt topical antibiotic prophylaxis and cycloplegia, with ophthalmology follow-up.  
Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology  
Recommendations: Prescribe a topical broad-spectrum antibiotic with antipseudomonal coverage (e.g., fluoroquinolone such as moxifloxacin or ciprofloxacin) given the contact lens use and metallic foreign body mechanism; administer a cycloplegic agent (e.g., cyclopentolate or homatropine) for ciliary spasm pain; provide oral analgesics for pain control; do not patch the eye, as patching is contraindicated in contact lens wearers due to increased infection risk; advise the patient to refrain from contact lens use until the epithelial defect is fully healed; check tetanus immunization status and update if indicated for a metal injury; refer to ophthalmology for follow-up within 24–48 hours; instruct the patient to return immediately for worsening pain, decreased vision, or purulent discharge.  
Notes: Contact lens wearers with corneal abrasions are at high risk for Pseudomonas keratitis; avoid patching and ensure antipseudomonal antibiotic coverage. A negative Seidel test excludes an open globe, but high-velocity metal injury warrants consideration of an intraocular foreign body via dilated exam or imaging.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe pain, coldness, and numbness in his left leg that started approximately 3 hours ago while sitting at home. He has a history of atrial fibrillation and was recently taken off warfarin due to a GI bleed. On examination, the left leg is pale and cool to the touch from the mid-thigh distally. Vital signs: T 36.9C, HR 88 (irregularly irregular), RR 16, BP 148/86, SpO2 97%. Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent by palpation and Doppler. Left popliteal pulse is faintly detectable. The left calf is tender with decreased sensation and the patient is unable to dorsiflex or plantarflex the left foot. Right leg pulses are palpable and symmetric. CT angiography shows abrupt occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery.
baseline_protocol:
Age: 68
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset of severe pain, coldness, and numbness in the left leg of 3 hours duration, with a pale, cool limb and absent distal pulses.
Analysis: The patient presents with acute limb ischemia of the left lower extremity. Strongest supporting facts include the acute onset of pain, coldness, and numbness; a pale, cool leg from the mid-thigh distally; absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses with a faint popliteal pulse; decreased sensation and motor weakness (inability to dorsiflex/plantarflex); and CT angiography demonstrating abrupt occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery. The history of atrial fibrillation (confirmed by irregularly irregular heart rate) and recent cessation of warfarin strongly support an embolic etiology. The presence of sensory and motor deficits indicates severe, limb-threatening ischemia (Rutherford class IIb). Main differential considerations include acute embolic occlusion (most likely given AF), acute in-situ thrombosis of a diseased vessel, and aortic or peripheral dissection; phlegmasia cerulea dolens is less likely given the arterial occlusion on imaging.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Bedside Doppler (already used); urgent blood tests including CBC, coagulation profile (INR/PTT), renal function, electrolytes, creatine kinase, and lactate; ECG to confirm rhythm; urgent vascular surgery evaluation. CT angiography has already been performed and confirms the diagnosis.
Conclusion: Acute left lower extremity ischemia due to embolic occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery in a patient with atrial fibrillation who was recently taken off anticoagulation. This is a limb-threatening emergency requiring urgent revascularization.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery
Recommendations: Immediate urgent vascular surgery consultation for emergent revascularization (embolectomy/thrombectomy). Administer systemic heparin anticoagulation, carefully weighing the risk of recurrent bleeding given the recent GI bleed versus the need to prevent thrombus propagation. Given the motor and sensory deficits, prepare for possible fasciotomy to treat or prevent compartment syndrome. Restore long-term anticoagulation (warfarin or a DOAC) once the bleeding risk is reassessed and controlled. Monitor closely for reperfusion injury, rhabdomyolysis, and acute kidney injury after revascularization.
Notes: The recent GI bleed significantly complicates anticoagulation decisions; the balance between bleeding risk and limb salvage must be individualized. The presence of motor and sensory deficits marks this as Rutherford class IIb ischemia, requiring intervention within hours to prevent irreversible tissue loss.
